newsitem.title: CANADA: Thiessen sees stronger Canadian dollar in long run.
newsitem.headline: Thiessen sees stronger Canadian dollar in long run.

text.p: Bank of Canada Governor Gordon Thiessen on Tuesday forecast a stronger Canadian dollar over the long run.

He also predicted Canada's current account, which in the second quarter showed a surplus for the first time in a decade, would once again be in the black in the third quarter. It is to be released on Friday.
Speaking to reporters after parliamentary testimony, the governor said the bank was "reasonably content" with the current level of its Monetary Conditions Index.

"I think the long-run trend -- given the fact that our inflation rate is lower than the United States inflation rate, given that our economy is weak and will pick up, given that the rest of the world is probably going to pick up somewhat, and that tends to lead to somewhat higher commodity prices -- you put all of that together, and you do get, I think, some strong factors suggesting an upward trend in the Canadian dollar," Thiessen said.
The governor also forecast that the Canadian gross domestic product would grow by four percent during 1997, as measured by fourth quarter 1997 over the same period 1996.

He repeated his prediction of three percent growth in gross domestic product in the second half of this year -- measured by the fourth quarter over the second quarter and turned into an annual rate. Third quarter GDP figures are to be announced on Friday.
One of the targets the central bank follows is its Monetary Conditions Index, which has moved consistently lower to -5.63 on November 20 from -3.22 a year earlier.
Asked if he was satisfied with its current level, he said: "We don't have a terribly precise target for it, because the thing can bounce around as the exchange rate moves around."
He added, however: "But I think you can judge that if we don't make any moves that we're reasonably content with the general range that it's in."

The Bank of Canada and the government has agreed to shoot for a core rate of inflation of one to three percent for the medium term. Asked when this would be made a long-term goal, he said: "The agreement that we have with the minister of finance, with the government, is that we are going to make a decision about the targets by the end of 1998.

"I don't think anybody is sitting there currently worrying about what that's going to be...I think most people see that we've been within the targets for quite a while and they expect us to stay within the targets."

On the issue of whether the differential of Canadian long-term yields over their U.S. counterparts could be expected to fall further, he noted that U.S. financial markets were the most liquid in the world and people would always pay a premium for 30-year U.S. Treasury securities.
"I really find it difficult to say if there's more room for those differentials to narrow or not. I don't know," he said.
